title: firewalld — Zone, Service, Port
lead: Listening is not the same as reachable: learn to read firewalld, change rules safely (runtime vs permanent) and meet ufw, the Debian/Ubuntu counterpart.
objectives: You check whether firewalld is running and read the default and active zones.
You explain runtime vs `--permanent` and what `--reload` does.
You open and close services and ports, and test rules safely with `--timeout`.
You write a simple rich rule for one source network.
You use ufw on Ubuntu and always allow SSH before enabling it.

sections.title: Zones, services, ports
body: With `ss` you see that a program listens. Whether others can reach it depends on the firewall in between. **firewalld** (Rocky/Alma/RHEL/Fedora) sorts every network interface into a **zone**: a trust level with its own list of allowed services and ports. `public` is the usual default; `trusted` allows everything, `drop` silently discards everything.

A **service** is a predefined bundle (`ssh` = 22/tcp, `http` = 80/tcp, `https` = 443/tcp). A **port** is an explicit number such as `8080/tcp`. Use a service when one exists, a port for non-standard numbers.
Always read before you change: first the state, then the zone, then the whole list.

commands.what: Prints running or not running.
commands.where: As the very first check on a Rocky/Alma VM.
commands.why: If the daemon is stopped, all other firewall-cmd commands fail.

commands.what: Shows the zone used for new interfaces.
commands.why: Rules without `--zone` go to the default zone.

commands.what: Lists zones that currently have interfaces or sources.
commands.where: When you wonder which zone really handles your traffic.
commands.why: The default zone can differ from the active one on an interface.

commands.what: Shows services, ports, rich rules and interfaces of a zone.
commands.why: Verify first, change, verify again.

sections.tip: `--list-all` shows the runtime state. Add `--permanent` to see what is stored on disk.

sections.title: Runtime vs permanent, --reload, --timeout
body: firewalld has two configurations. **Runtime** is active right now and is lost on `--reload` or reboot. **Permanent** is written to disk and survives reboots, but `--permanent` alone does **not** change the running firewall.

Typical safe workflow: test in runtime with `--timeout`, check, and only then write it permanently and run `--reload`. `--reload` applies the permanent configuration and **discards runtime-only rules**.
A good test: if a rule works in runtime and you want to keep it, use `firewall-cmd --runtime-to-permanent`.

commands.what: Adds a runtime rule that disappears after 60 seconds.
commands.why: If you made a mistake, it fixes itself.

commands.what: Writes the rule to disk only; not active yet.
commands.where: For rules that must survive a reboot.
commands.why: Runtime and permanent are separate lists.

commands.what: Loads the permanent configuration into runtime.
commands.why: Activates permanent rules; runtime-only rules are dropped.

commands.what: Saves the current runtime rules as permanent.
commands.where: After you tested a rule and it works.
commands.why: No need to type the rule twice.

sections.warn: Take a VM snapshot first (module 0.2). On a remote machine keep a **second SSH session open** while you change firewall rules.
sections.danger: SSH lockout: never remove the `ssh` service from the active zone, never set the zone to `drop`, and never run `--panic-on` over SSH. Your session dies at once and you only get back in through the VM console. Test with `--timeout`, verify with `--list-all`, and keep the order: verify, change, verify.

sections.title: Opening and closing ports and services
body: For a web app on port 8080 use `--add-port=8080/tcp`. To close it again use `--remove-port` or `--remove-service`. Remember: every `--permanent` change needs `--reload`.
A port in the firewall does not start the program. Check with `ss` that something listens. On Rocky/Alma with SELinux a non-standard port may also need a label (module 6.2).

commands.what: Lists all predefined service names.
commands.where: To find the right service name.
commands.why: A service is clearer than a bare number.

commands.what: Opens 8080/tcp permanently (after reload).
commands.why: Services only cover standard ports.

commands.what: Lists explicitly opened ports.
commands.why: Confirms the rule is active in runtime.

commands.what: Removes the port rule from the permanent config.
commands.why: Open ports you no longer need are risk.

sections.tip: Write the commands into a small script first and read it twice before you run it.

sections.title: Rich rules (briefly)
body: A **rich rule** adds conditions: source address, port, protocol and action (`accept`, `reject`, `drop`). Example: allow PostgreSQL (5432) only from the network `192.168.1.0/24`.
Quote the whole rule in single quotes and the values inside in double quotes. Add `--timeout` while testing.

commands.what: Adds a conditional rule.
commands.where: When a port must be open only for one network.
commands.why: More precise than opening the port for everyone.
commands.example: sudo firewall-cmd --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.168.1.0/24" port port="5432" protocol="tcp" accept' --timeout=60

commands.what: Shows the rich rules of the zone.
commands.why: Rich rules are not shown in `--list-services`.

commands.what: Removes a rich rule; give the exact same text.
commands.where: When the exception is no longer needed.
commands.why: Keeps the rule set small.
commands.example: sudo firewall-cmd --remove-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.168.1.0/24" port port="5432" protocol="tcp" accept'

sections.warn: A `reject` or `drop` rule for your own admin network can cut your SSH session. Use `--timeout` and keep a second session.

sections.title: Debian/Ubuntu: ufw
body: Ubuntu uses **ufw** (Uncomplicated Firewall). It is usually installed but **disabled**. The golden rule: **allow SSH first, enable second**. `ufw enable` with default `deny incoming` and no SSH rule locks you out.
`OpenSSH` is an application profile, equal to 22/tcp. Rules are active at once and persistent; there is no runtime/permanent split.

commands.what: Allows SSH (22/tcp).
commands.why: Prevents locking yourself out.

commands.what: Turns the firewall on and keeps it on after reboot.
commands.why: The default policy blocks incoming traffic.

commands.what: Shows state, default policy and rules.
commands.why: Check that 22/tcp is ALLOW.

commands.what: Removes an allow rule.
commands.where: When a port is no longer needed.
commands.why: Keeps exposure small.

sections.danger: Never run `ufw enable` over SSH before `ufw allow OpenSSH` (or `ufw allow 22/tcp`). If your SSH port is not 22, allow that port. Snapshot the VM first.

sections.title: Reading listening ports and logs
body: Before you open anything, find out what really listens: `ss -tulpn` on the VM. In the simulator you practise with sample files in `~/fw`: `ss.txt` is a fake `ss` output, `blocked.log` a fake firewall log.
With `grep`, `cut`, `sort` and `uniq -c` you can count and rank. This is the same technique you use on real logs.

commands.what: Lists listening TCP/UDP sockets with the process.
commands.where: To see which ports are in use.
commands.why: Open firewall ports without a listener are pointless.

commands.what: Counts matching lines.
commands.why: A fast number instead of scrolling.

commands.what: Extracts a column and counts equal values.
commands.why: Shows the noisiest source at a glance.

commands.what: Finds lines ignoring case.
commands.where: To read ALLOW rules in a ufw status file.
commands.why: No need to know the exact capitalisation.

sections.tip: The sample scripts in `~/fw` are only text files. They are never executed against a real firewall.

t01.text: Go to the practice folder with `cd ~/fw`.
t01.hint: The prompt shows the new directory.

t02.text: Show the fake zone output with `cat public.txt`.

t03.text: Find the services line with `grep ssh public.txt`.

t04.text: Write a safe test command into `test_http.sh`: `firewall-cmd --add-service=http --timeout=60`. Use `echo "..." > test_http.sh`.
t04.hint: `--timeout` makes the rule vanish by itself.

t05.hint: Use a single `>` to create the file.

t06.text: Append `firewall-cmd --reload` to `perm_http.sh` (permanent rules need a reload).

t07.text: Predict, then check: how many listening sockets are in `ss.txt`? Run `grep -c LISTEN ss.txt`.

t08.text: Predict the output of `cut -d: -f1 active.txt | sort` (zone names, sorted), then run it.
t08.hint: The field before the colon is the zone.

t09.text: `broken.sh` has a typo and forgets `--permanent`. Fix it so it contains `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http`.

t10.text: `ufw-setup.sh` enables ufw before allowing SSH — a lockout! Rewrite it so `ufw allow OpenSSH` comes first, then `ufw enable`.

t11.text: Mini project: write `web.sh` with three lines: permanent `http`, permanent `https`, then `firewall-cmd --reload`.

t12.text: Challenge: find the noisiest blocked source in `blocked.log`. Extract column 3, sort, count with `uniq -c`, rank, keep the first line and save it to `top.txt`.

t13.text: Challenge: write a rich rule into `rich.sh`: `firewall-cmd --add-rich-rule=...` that accepts tcp port 5432 only from `192.168.1.0/24`.
t13.hint: Single quotes around the rule, escaped double quotes inside a double-quoted `echo`.

t14.text: Ticket: The app on port 8080 is not reachable from outside and must survive a reboot. Write `fix.sh` with the permanent port rule for `8080/tcp` and the reload. Do not touch ssh.

t15.text: Ticket: A new Ubuntu server needs SSH and web access, then the firewall must be on. Write `ufw.sh`: allow OpenSSH, allow 80/tcp, then enable — in a lockout-safe order.
t15.hint: `ufw enable` must be the last line.

t16.text: Predict: how many lines in `history.txt` contain `permanent`? Then verify with `grep -c permanent history.txt`.

t17.text: Read the ufw rules with `grep -i allow ufw-status.txt`. Is 22/tcp allowed?

t18.text: Write a runtime test for port 9090 into `port.sh`: `firewall-cmd --add-port=9090/tcp --timeout=60`.
t18.hint: Same pattern as for the service.

vm.intro: Use a Rocky/Alma VM for v01–v04 and an Ubuntu VM for v05. Take a snapshot first (module 0.2) and work from the VM console or keep a second SSH session open.

v01.title: Read the firewall state
v01.text: Check that firewalld runs, read the default zone and the full list. Paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
sudo firewall-cmd --state
sudo firewall-cmd --get-default-zone
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all
blocks.expected:
running
public
public
  interfaces: enp0s3
public (active)
  services: cockpit dhcpv6-client ssh
  ports:

differs: If it says `not running`: `sudo systemctl enable --now firewalld`.
On Ubuntu firewalld is usually not installed; use ufw (v05).
Your zone or interface name may differ (`enp0s3`, `ens160`).

v02.title: Runtime rule with a timeout
v02.text: Add http for 120 seconds, list the services, wait, list again. The rule vanishes by itself.
differs: `ssh` must still be in the list; if not, add it back immediately: `sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=ssh`.

v03.title: Permanent vs runtime
v03.text: Write http permanently, compare the permanent and runtime list before and after `--reload`.

blocks.cmd:
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http
sudo firewall-cmd --list-services --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --list-services
blocks.expected:
success
cockpit dhcpv6-client http ssh
success
cockpit dhcpv6-client http ssh

differs: After `--reload` the runtime list now equals the permanent list.
Without `--reload` the runtime list would not contain `http` (unless v02 is still active).

v04.title: Open and close a port
v04.text: Open 8080/tcp permanently, reload and check. Then remove it again and reload.

blocks.cmd:
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8080/tcp
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --list-ports
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --remove-port=8080/tcp
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --list-ports

differs: The last `--list-ports` output should be empty.

v05.title: Ubuntu: ufw with SSH first
v05.text: On Ubuntu allow SSH first, then enable ufw and read the status. Paste the status output.

blocks.cmd:
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status verbose
blocks.expected:
Status: active
Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing)

To            Action      From
22/tcp        ALLOW IN    Anywhere

differs: ufw may ask `Command may disrupt existing ssh connections` — fine, because SSH is allowed.
If ufw is not found: `sudo apt install ufw`.

q1.q: What does `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http` do on its own?
options: It opens http immediately and for good
It writes the rule to disk, active only after `--reload`
q1.explain: `--permanent` only changes the stored configuration. The running firewall changes after `--reload`.

q2.q: You are connected over SSH to a new Ubuntu server. What must come before `ufw enable`?
q2.explain: ufw blocks incoming traffic by default. Without an SSH rule you lock yourself out.

options: The runtime rule disappears after 60 seconds
The rule is permanent for 60 days
It waits 60 seconds before adding it
It limits connections to 60 per minute
q3.explain: Timeout rules are runtime only and remove themselves — a safety net for tests.

q4.q: What happens to runtime-only rules on `firewall-cmd --reload`?
q4.explain: `--reload` reloads the permanent configuration and drops runtime-only changes.

summary: firewalld sorts interfaces into zones; `--list-all` shows what a zone allows.
Runtime is active now; `--permanent` is stored and needs `--reload`; `--reload` drops runtime-only rules.
Test with `--timeout`, verify before and after, keep a second SSH session and a snapshot.
Use services for standard ports and `--add-port` for the rest; rich rules limit a rule to a source network.
On Ubuntu: `ufw allow OpenSSH` first, `ufw enable` second.

glossary.meaning: A trust level with its own allowed services and ports; each interface belongs to one zone.
A predefined firewalld bundle of ports, such as http = 80/tcp.
An explicit number plus protocol, for example 8080/tcp.
The configuration active right now; lost on reload or reboot.
The configuration stored on disk; applied by `--reload` or reboot.
Loads the permanent configuration and discards runtime-only rules.
Makes a runtime rule expire automatically after the given time.
A conditional rule with source, port, protocol and action.
Uncomplicated Firewall, the default front end on Ubuntu.
Losing your own SSH access because of a firewall change.
